items.caseName: Novartis AG v. Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax (International Taxation), Circle 3(3)(1)
items.coram: Beena Pillai (Judicial Member) and Arun Khodpia (Accountant Member)
items.headline: Novartis trademark assignment gains are not royalty; ₹433.14 crore addition deleted
items.text: The Tribunal deleted a ₹433.14 crore addition the Revenue had taxed as royalty on Novartis AG's assignment of three Indian trademarks to USV, Cipla and Eris. It found that the deeds transferred ownership of the marks together with goodwill rather than a mere right to use, and that a trademark sale need not carry the whole corporate identity, house marks or packaging. The gains were treated as alienation of property under Article 13(6) of the India–Switzerland DTAA and held taxable only in Switzerland.

items.caseName: Yes Bank Ltd. v. Rajesh Madan
items.coram: Justice Anupinder Singh Grewal (President) and Ravindra Chaturvedi (Technical Member)
items.headline: Proposed assignment of debt to an ARC does not bar insolvency against a personal guarantor
items.text: The Delhi Bench admitted Yes Bank's Section 95 application against the personal guarantor of Johnson Watch Company over a claimed debt of about ₹17.07 crore, and appointed a resolution professional. It held that the bank's unproven talks to assign the debt to an asset reconstruction company did not stop the proceedings. It also rejected the guarantor's objections about invocation of the guarantee through the SARFAESI notice and about the pending CIRP against the principal borrower.

items.caseName: M/s Prithvi Asset Reconstruction & Securitization Company v. M/s Alpine Wineries Pvt Ltd.
items.coram: Sunil Kumar Aggarwal (Judicial Member) and Radhakrishna Sreepada (Technical Member)
items.headline: Alpine Wineries' liquidation ended after ₹49 crore settlement with financial creditors
items.text: The Bengaluru Bench allowed a former director's application to end the liquidation of Alpine Wineries after both financial creditors accepted one-time settlements totalling about ₹49 crore. Since Section 12A could not be applied mechanically once liquidation had started, the Bench used its inherent powers under Section 60(5) read with Rule 11 and cited the preference for revival over liquidation. The liquidator was told to hand the assets and records back to the former board, and the Bench noted that other stakeholders' claims must still be protected.

items.caseName: Rajeev Sharma; Neeraj Saluja v. Rajeev Sharma
items.coram: Khetrabasi Biswal (Judicial Member) and Kaushalendra Kumar Singh (Technical Member)
items.headline: SEL Textiles liquidation deferred; fresh resolution process to finish within 120 days
items.text: The Chandigarh Bench declined to order liquidation of SEL Textiles for now, holding that the rejection of earlier resolution plans does not by itself rule out revival. Because the company's four manufacturing units depend on one another and could lose value if sold separately, the resolution professional must invite fresh plans for the business as a single undertaking. A new Form G must be issued and the process completed within 120 days.

items.caseName: Raj Kumar Jindal & Vivek Aggarwal v. SRS Real Estate Ltd
items.coram: Khetrabasi Biswal (Judicial Member) and Kaushalendra Kumar Singh (Technical Member)
items.headline: Payments to group entities do not automatically make homebuyers financial creditors of the debtor
items.text: The Chandigarh Bench held that money paid to associate entities does not by itself create a financial debt of the corporate debtor unless it is linked to the debtor's liability. Since the record did not show that the ₹54 lakh reached SRS Real Estate, the Bench sent the claims back to the resolution professional to verify the evidence again. It also held that the claims could not be rejected only for being filed late, and kept the applicants under 'Other Creditors' in the meantime.

items.coram: Praveen Gupta (Judicial Member) and Ashish Verma (Technical Member)
items.headline: Redmil Business Mall's own insolvency plea admitted over ₹9.41 crore default
items.text: The Allahabad Bench admitted Redmil Business Mall's own Section 10 application. It found a default of about ₹9.41 crore owed to two operational creditors and one financial creditor, above the Section 4 threshold. The Bench started CIRP, declared a moratorium and appointed an interim resolution professional.

items.caseName: M/s Ambika Traders and Ors v. Shree Basaveshwar Sugars Limited and Ors
items.coram: Sunil Kumar Aggarwal (Judicial Member) and Radhakrishna Sreepada (Technical Member)
items.headline: Holding shares alone does not let shareholders represent the company in court
items.text: The Bengaluru Bench dismissed a plea by shareholders holding about 22% of the company's capital to represent it in a High Court challenge to an arbitral award of roughly ₹52.71 crore. The applicants were not directors and had no authorisation from the company. The Bench held that their pending oppression petition did not give them authority either, and that granting the plea would effectively displace the board.

items.caseName: Ashok Kumar Singh v. M/s Safecon Lifesciences Private Limited
items.coram: Ajeet Singh (Judicial Member) and Vivek Kumar (Technical Member)
items.headline: ITC cannot be denied on a bare allegation that the supplier is bogus
items.text: The Agra Bench dismissed the Department's appeal and upheld the order setting aside a ₹3.83 lakh ITC demand and penalty. It held that a supplier's alleged bogus status cannot justify denying credit without examining the buyer's invoices, e-way bills, payment and transport records. The later restoration of the supplier's cancelled registration, which the Revenue did not contest, also weakened the allegation.

items.caseName: Associated Cashews v. Commissioner of CGST, Thiruvananthapuram
items.coram: Subramanya Rayaprol (Vice-President) and Ramamoorthi Sriram (Technical Member)
items.headline: Cashew exporter gets refund of IGST paid twice because of a GSTR-3B reporting error
items.text: The exporter had shown its export sales in the domestic column of GSTR-3B. This blocked the automatic refund, so it paid IGST a second time. The Bench allowed all three appeals and directed a refund of the original payment of about ₹19.79 lakh, holding that the authorities could not keep excess tax caused by a documented clerical mistake.

items.caseName: Vikas Ashokkumar Masand v. The Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax
items.coram: Dr. B.R.R. Kumar (Vice-President) and Tapas Ram Misra (Judicial Member)
items.headline: Petrol pump's demonetisation-period cash receipts not unexplained; ₹34.40 lakh addition deleted
items.text: The Bench deleted a Section 69A addition of about ₹34.40 lakh for AY 2017-18 against a petrol pump operator. It held that cash received from customers during demonetisation cannot be treated as unexplained only because debtor confirmations were missing, when the entries were in the books and no defects were found. It also held that using Section 68 as an alternative ground without giving the assessee a fair chance to respond was not acceptable.

items.caseName: Azure Knowledge Corporation Pvt. Ltd. v. The Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax
items.coram: Dr. B.R.R. Kumar (Vice-President) and Tapas Ram Misra (Judicial Member)
items.headline: Azure Knowledge's ₹2.46 crore software capitalisation dispute sent back for fresh check
items.text: The Bench set aside the CIT(A)'s order and sent the matter back to the Assessing Officer. The officer must check whether about ₹2.46 crore in software customisation and development costs is genuine and can be capitalised. The officer must also check whether any amount was disallowed twice by comparing the returns, the intimation, the tax audit report and the assessment order, after giving the company a hearing.
